title: Tap to call: make it easy on a phone
facts: Many people look up local businesses on their phones.
A phone number that is plain text forces the visitor to copy and paste it.
A tap-to-call button near the top of every page lets a customer reach you in one tap.
Check your own site on your phone: can you find the call button without scrolling?

title: Your Google Business Profile: keep it complete
facts: Google shows your profile in local search and on maps, often before your website.
Correct hours, phone number, service area and business categories help customers trust it.
Real photos of your work and your team make the listing more useful than a bare name and address.
If your hours or services changed, update the profile the same day.

title: Answer your Google reviews
facts: Replying to reviews shows future customers that a real person runs the business.
Thank people for good reviews in a sentence or two, and mention the actual job when it fits.
For a poor review, reply calmly, offer to fix it, and take the details offline.
Never argue in public; readers judge the reply as much as the review.

title: Ask happy customers for a review
facts: Most happy customers never think to leave a review unless asked.
Ask right after the job is done and the customer is pleased.
Send the direct review link by text or email so it takes one tap.
One short, polite request is enough; do not offer payment or discounts for reviews.

title: Put your city where searchers look
facts: People search with a city name, such as heating repair in Ocala.
Your homepage title and main heading should say what you do and where you do it.
Vague titles like Home or Welcome waste the most important line Google reads.
List the towns you serve on a page of their own instead of one long list in the footer.

title: Say what you do in the first five seconds
facts: A visitor should know what you do, where, and how to reach you without scrolling.
A clear headline, a phone number and a button for a quote or booking cover that.
Slideshows and long welcome speeches push those basics out of view.
Ask a friend to look at your homepage for five seconds, then ask what you do.

title: A slow site loses people before they see it
facts: Visitors on a phone often leave if a page takes too long to show.
Very large images are one of the most common reasons local sites load slowly.
Resizing and compressing photos before uploading them is usually a quick fix.
Free tools such as Google PageSpeed Insights show where a page is slow.

title: The little padlock matters
facts: A site served over HTTPS shows a padlock; without it, browsers can show a Not secure warning.
A warning on a contact page can scare away a customer who was about to call or fill in a form.
Most hosting companies offer HTTPS at no extra cost.
If you see a warning on your own site, ask your web provider to fix it.

title: Look at your own site on your phone
facts: Open your site on a phone, not just a computer.
Check that text is readable without zooming and nothing runs off the side of the screen.
Check that buttons are easy to tap with a thumb.
Try the contact form yourself and make sure the message actually reaches you.

title: An old copyright year says nobody is home
facts: A footer that still says 2018 can make a business look closed or neglected.
Updating the year, or using a year that updates itself, takes minutes.
Fresh photos, current hours and a recent blog post send the same signal.
Customers often decide in seconds whether a business is still active.

title: Real photos beat generic ones
facts: Photos of your real trucks, team and finished jobs help customers picture working with you.
Generic images could be on any company's site, so they add little trust.
Take photos on a modern phone in good daylight; you do not need a studio.
Add a short caption saying what the job was and where.

title: Make it easy to get in touch
facts: Every page should offer a way to contact you: a phone number, a button or a short form.
Keep forms short; name, phone and a few words about the job is often enough.
Reply quickly; a fast answer often wins the job over a slightly cheaper competitor.
Test your form every few months to make sure messages still arrive.

title: Give each service its own page
facts: One page that lists every service tells Google and visitors very little about each one.
A separate page for each main service lets you explain it, show examples and answer common questions.
Include the towns you serve on those pages in natural sentences.
Link between related service pages so visitors can keep reading.

title: Answer common questions on your site
facts: Customers ask the same questions again and again: pricing, timing, what is included.
Writing the answers on your site saves phone time and builds trust.
Use the exact words customers use when they call you.
Short, honest answers work better than long sales copy.

title: Link your website and social pages together
facts: Customers often check a business's Facebook page before calling.
Link your social pages from your website, and link your website from your profiles.
Keep contact details identical everywhere: the same name, address and phone number.
An active page with recent posts is better than an abandoned one.

title: Local search starts with consistency
facts: Your business name, address and phone number should match across your website, Google and directories.
Mismatched details can confuse both customers and search engines.
Claim your listing on the main directories and check them once a year.
Small corrections add up over time.

title: Why a small business blog can help
facts: A blog lets you answer real customer questions in your own words.
Each helpful post is another page that can show up when someone searches for that problem.
One useful post a month is better than ten posts and then silence.
Write about jobs you actually did and questions customers actually asked.

title: A website is your hardest-working employee
facts: It answers the phone at night and on weekends, and it never takes a day off.
It only works if visitors can quickly see what you do and how to reach you.
Treat it like a truck or a tool: keep it maintained and updated.
Review it twice a year: photos, hours, services and contact details.

title: Make your site easy to read
facts: Low contrast text and tiny fonts are hard for many people, especially on a bright phone screen.
Use dark text on a light background, or the reverse, with strong contrast.
Keep body text at a comfortable size and leave space between lines.
Write descriptive alt text for important images.

title: Make booking a one-step action
facts: Every extra step between I need a quote and I asked for one loses some customers.
A booking or quote button that stays visible on a phone helps.
Say what happens next, such as we will call you within one business day.
Only promise a response time you can keep.
